#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
# fonts ----
library(extrafont)
library(sysfonts)
source("_common.R")

showtext::showtext_auto()

ggplot2::theme_set(fmggp2::theme_furby(

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(1998)
furby_chatter <- tibble(
  hour_id = 1:300,
  language = rep(c("Furbish", "English"), times = c(180, 120))) |>
  mutate(language = factor(language, levels = c("Furbish", "English")),
         words_per_hour = round(if_else(language == "Furbish",
           rnorm(n(), mean = 45, sd = 8),
           rnorm(n(), mean = 30, sd = 10))))
labs_ovrlp_density <- labs(
  subtitle = "position = 'identity'",
  x = "Words per hour",
  fill = "Language")
ggp2_ovrlp_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
       aes(x = words_per_hour,
           fill = language)) +
      geom_density(alpha = 1/3)

ovrlp_density <- ggp2_ovrlp_density +
  labs_ovrlp_density +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

labs_stack_density <- labs(
  subtitle = "position = 'stack'",
  x = "Words per hour",
  fill = "Language")
ggp2_stack_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
       aes(x = words_per_hour,
           after_stat(count),
           fill = language)) +
      geom_density(position = "stack",
                   alpha = 1/3)
stack_density <- ggp2_stack_density +
  labs_stack_density +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
ovrlp_density + stack_density +
    patchwork::plot_layout(ncol = 1)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a categorical variable**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

## Description

Density plots are [*smoothed version(s) of  histogram(s)*](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html). They can are great for comparing the distributions of a continuous variable across the levels of a categorical variable.

`geom_density()` creates a kernel density estimate. The default `position` argument is `"identity"`, which takes the data as is. However, we can change `position` to `"stack"` to display overlapping distributions.

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Install packages.
:::


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Furby was the must have toy of 1998. Out of the box it spoke "Furbish," and the longer you played with it, the more English it seemed to learn. We'll simulate 300 hours of Furby chatter: 180 hours spent mostly in Furbish and 120 hours mostly in English. Each language gets its own normal distribution of words per hour (`rnorm()`), and Furbish hours are both chattier and more consistent. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 300 hours every time you run the code below.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1998)
furby_chatter <- tibble(
  hour_id = 1:300,
  language = rep(c("Furbish", "English"), times = c(180, 120))) |>
  mutate(language = factor(language, levels = c("Furbish", "English")),
         words_per_hour = round(if_else(language == "Furbish",
           rnorm(n(), mean = 45, sd = 8),
           rnorm(n(), mean = 30, sd = 10))))
dplyr::glimpse(furby_chatter)
```
:::

## Distribution

Overlapping and stacked density plots can tell two different stories about the same data. By default, each group's curve covers an area of 1, which hides the fact that one group might be much bigger than the other. Our two languages aren't the same size (180 hours vs. 120), so the choice matters here. Below we'll move from the hours, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first five hours (all in Furbish).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(furby_chatter, 5)
```
:::

These five hours range from 23 to 57 words. The summary below compares the two languages: Furbish has more hours, more words per hour on average, and a smaller standard deviation.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
furby_chatter |> 
  group_by(language) |> 
  summarise(hours = n(), mean = mean(words_per_hour), 
            sd = sd(words_per_hour))
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

A bar model shows the two groups as parts of all 300 hours. Furbish takes up 60% of the bar and English takes up 40%.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_bar_model_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| fig-asp: 0.45
furby_chatter |> 
  count(language) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = "300 hours", fill = language)) + 
  geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) + 
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "#2D1B4E", 
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE)) + 
  labs(x = "Hours", y = NULL, fill = "Language")
```
:::

The two graphs below show why the bar model matters. On the left, the default densities each cover an area of 1, so the English curve looks almost as big as the Furbish curve. On the right, `after_stat(count)` scales each curve by its number of hours, so the Furbish curve is 1.5 times the size of the English curve, just like the bar model.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(furby_chatter, aes(x = words_per_hour, fill = language)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 1/2) + 
  labs(title = "Area of 1 each", x = "Words per hour", 
    fill = "Language") + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplot(furby_chatter, aes(x = words_per_hour, after_stat(count), 
    fill = language)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 1/2) + 
  labs(title = "Scaled by hours", x = "Words per hour", y = "count",
    fill = "Language") + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Each language has its own [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution), and the two are mixed in proportion to their number of hours:

$$
f(x) = 0.6 \cdot \text{Normal}(x;\, 45, 8) + 0.4 \cdot \text{Normal}(x;\, 30, 10)
$$

`geom_density()` estimates each group's curve so that its area is 1 (each $\text{Normal}$ term on its own). `after_stat(count)` multiplies each curve by its group size, so the two curves have areas of 180 and 120. Stacking those count curves (`position = "stack"`) adds them together into $300 \times f(x)$, the curve for all 300 hours. Try making the two groups the same size in `rep()` and the two graphs above will look almost identical.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::



  -   Create labels with `labs()`

  -   Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  -   Map the `words_per_hour` to the `x` and `language` to `fill`

  -   Add the `geom_density()`

  -   Set the `alpha` to `1/3` (to handle the overlapping areas)

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_ovrlp_density
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_ovrlp_density <- labs(
  title = "Furby chatter",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "Words per hour",
  fill = "Language")
ggp2_ovrlp_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
       aes(x = words_per_hour,
           fill = language)) +
      geom_density(alpha = 1/3)
ggp2_ovrlp_density +
  labs_ovrlp_density
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

::: {.column-margin}
*A downside of density plots is the lack of interpretability of the `y` axis*
:::


Make density area slightly transparent to handle over-plotting.

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_ovrlp_density
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_ovrlp_density <- labs(
  title = "Furby chatter",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "Words per hour",
  fill = "Language")
ggp2_ovrlp_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
       aes(x = words_per_hour,
           fill = language)) +
      geom_density(alpha = 1/3)
ggp2_ovrlp_density +
  labs_ovrlp_density
```

## More info

`ggplot2` has multiple options for overlapping density plots, so which one to use will depend on how you'd like to display the relative distributions in your data. We'll cover three options below:

### `"stack"`

If we change the `position` to `"stack"` we can see the smoothed estimates are 'stacked' on top each other (and the `y` axis shifts slightly).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{r}
#| label: code_graph_stack_density
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_stack_density <- labs(
    title = "Furby chatter",
    caption = "Simulated data",
    x = "Words per hour",
    fill = "Language")
ggp2_stack_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
    mapping = aes(x = words_per_hour,
               fill = language)) +
    geom_density(position = "stack",
                 alpha = 1 / 3)
ggp2_stack_density +
    labs_stack_density
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"}
Setting `position` to `'stack'` [loses marginal densities](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html#ref-examples)
:::

### `after_stat(count)`


If we include `after_stat(count)` as one of our mapped aesthetics, the mapping is postponed until after statistical transformation, and uses the [*`density * n` instead of the default density*](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html#computed-variables).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_after_stat_density
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_after_stat_density <- labs(
  title = "Furby chatter",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "Words per hour",
  fill = "Language")
ggp2_after_stat_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
       aes(x = words_per_hour,
           after_stat(count),
           fill = language)) +
      geom_density(position = "stack",
                   alpha = 1/3)
ggp2_after_stat_density +
  labs_after_stat_density
```
:::


Adding [`after_stat(count)`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html#computed-variables) *'preserves marginal densities.'*, which result in more a interpretable `y` axis (depending on the audience)

### `"fill"`


Using `after_stat(count)` with `position = "fill"` creates in a conditional density estimate.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_fill_density
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_fill_density <- labs(
  title = "Furby chatter",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  x = "Words per hour",
  fill = "Language")
ggp2_fill_density <- ggplot(data = furby_chatter,
       aes(x = words_per_hour,
           after_stat(count),
           fill = language)) +
      geom_density(position = "fill",
                   alpha = 1/3)
ggp2_fill_density +
  labs_fill_density
```
:::


This results in a `y` axis ranging from 0-1, and the area filled with the relative proportional values.
